label: Qin Dynasty
pitch:
The Zhou era ended with a question none of its philosophers could answer in the abstract: which school of thought actually works? After five centuries of Warring States chaos — the same chaos that produced Confucius, Laozi, and the Hundred Schools — the state of Qin answered with Legalism. Shang Yang's reforms stripped away aristocratic privilege, rewarded military killing with land and rank, and built the most efficient war machine the ancient world had seen. By 221 BCE, Qin's armies had swallowed the other six kingdoms, and a 38-year-old king named Ying Zheng renamed himself Qin Shi Huang: the First Emperor. What followed was the most radical political experiment in Chinese history — total standardization, centralized bureaucracy, the end of feudalism — and it lasted exactly fifteen years.

🔑 Key Facts:
• Shang Yang's Legalist reforms transformed Qin from a backward frontier state into a military superpower by replacing aristocratic birth with measurable merit — the same principle Han Feizi theorized in the Zhou era, now applied without limit
• The Battle of Changping (260 BCE) was the decisive turning point: Qin buried 400,000 Zhao prisoners alive, breaking the last state capable of resisting unification
• Qin Shi Huang (Ying Zheng) coined the title "Huangdi" (Emperor) by combining legendary sage-king honorifics — no existing title fit a ruler of all China, and every subsequent emperor used it for 2,132 years
• Standardization of writing meant a scholar from Shandong could read documents from Sichuan — the script the Qin imposed is the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, extending the Shang's 3,400-year writing tradition
• The Terracotta Army contains over 8,000 unique clay soldiers with individualized faces — a workforce in death to mirror the vast labor armies that built his empire in life
• The Great Wall connected existing frontier walls into a single defensive line — the concept of a northern barrier would define Chinese military strategy for two millennia
• The Burning of Books and Burying of Scholars targeted Confucian and historical texts that questioned Legalist orthodoxy — the first large-scale ideological censorship in Chinese history
• Li Si, the chancellor who implemented standardization, and Han Feizi, the theorist whose ideas built the empire, were classmates under the Confucian teacher Xunzi — Legalism's architects were trained by the tradition they replaced

🤔 Why It Matters: The Qin didn't just conquer China — they invented it as a unified state. Standardized script, weights, measures, axle widths, currency, and a road network replaced the patchwork of feudal kingdoms with a single administrative system. The bureaucratic model replaced aristocracy with trained officials loyal to the state. But the Qin's own Legalist logic destroyed them: a system built on fear and punishment couldn't survive a succession crisis, and the empire collapsed into rebellion within four years of the First Emperor's death. The Han dynasty that rose from the ashes kept every Qin institution — the bureaucracy, the script, the roads, the centralized governance — but softened the ideology with Confucian ethics, creating a synthesis of Legalist structure and Confucian virtue that would govern China for the next two thousand years.

🎲 Wild Card: Zhao Gao, the scheming eunuch who dominated the Second Emperor, brought a deer before the court and called it a horse. Officials who agreed survived; anyone who called it a deer was executed. The phrase 'pointing to a deer and calling it a horse' still means deliberate political gaslighting in Chinese today — and it captures perfectly why a system built entirely on power and fear was doomed to self-destruct.

details.label: Background
details.text: In 356 BCE, the state of Qin was a western backwater dismissed by the cultured eastern states as semi-barbarian. Duke Xiao invited reformers to transform Qin — and Shang Yang answered, remaking the state from the ground up with Legalist principles.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Shang Yang abolished aristocratic privilege, divided the country into administrative counties, and created a 20-rank military merit system. Soldiers advanced by collecting enemy heads — an army motivated by personal gain rather than feudal loyalty, and terrifyingly effective.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: Over the next century, Qin methodically weakened its rivals through war, diplomacy, and assassination. The Battle of Changping in 260 BCE, where Qin buried 400,000 Zhao prisoners, signaled to every remaining state that Qin's victory was inevitable.

details.label: Background
details.text: By 230 BCE, Ying Zheng had consolidated power after surviving assassination attempts and palace coups. He turned his generals loose on the remaining six kingdoms in a systematic campaign of conquest.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: Qin conquered the six kingdoms one by one over nine years: Han (230), Zhao (228), Wei (225), Chu (223), Yan (222), and finally Qi (221). Each conquest was preceded by bribery, betrayal, and strategic isolation before the military blow fell.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The speed and totality of conquest astonished contemporaries. A world of warring states that had fought for 250 years was united in less than a decade. Nothing like it had happened in Chinese history — and it would not be undone for the next two millennia.

details.label: Background
details.text: Qin Shi Huang (Ying Zheng) crowned himself the First Emperor and immediately set about transforming a war machine into a governing apparatus. His chancellor Li Si oversaw systematic standardization of everything: script, laws, roads, weights, and measures.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: The First Emperor connected existing walls into the Great Wall, built a road network of 6,800 km, and began the largest mausoleum in world history. He made six imperial tours to project his presence across the empire and suppress lingering regional identities.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: In 213 BCE, the Emperor ordered the burning of all books outside state-approved texts — eliminating the intellectual diversity of the Hundred Schools of Thought. The Han dynasty later reversed this, but the damage to pre-Qin texts was permanent.

details.label: Background
details.text: Qin Shi Huang died on his fifth imperial tour in 210 BCE. The eunuch Zhao Gao and chancellor Li Si suppressed news of his death long enough to forge a succession decree, passing the throne to the pliable younger son Huhai instead of the designated heir Fusu.

details.label: What Happened
details.text: The Second Emperor Qin Er Shi ruled through terror under Zhao Gao's manipulation. In 209 BCE, two conscripted peasants — Chen Sheng and Wu Guang — sparked the first uprising. Within months, a dozen rebel armies were in the field, including Xiang Yu and Liu Bang.

details.label: The Bigger Picture
details.text: The Qin collapsed in 206 BCE — just 15 years after unification. Xiang Yu's army burned Xianyang and executed the last Qin ruler. A four-year civil war between Xiang Yu and the peasant Liu Bang ended with Liu Bang founding the Han dynasty.

events.label: Shang Yang
events.description: The Legalist statesman who rebuilt Qin from the ground up, betting that clear law and ruthless incentives beat virtue every time. He served Duke Xiao as chief minister for two decades, and his system long outlived him.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Shang Yang wasn't his birth name. He was born Gongsun Yang in the small state of Wey around 390 BCE; "Shang" came later, from the fief of Shang that Qin granted him as a reward. The legend goes that to prove his new laws would actually be enforced, he planted a wooden pole at a city gate and promised gold to anyone who'd carry it to the other gate, a stunt to convince a skeptical public the state meant what it said. When he fell from power in 338 BCE and tried to flee, an innkeeper turned him away for lacking the identity papers his own laws required, so he was caught and torn apart by chariots, and his whole family was executed with him.

events.label: Duke Xiao of Qin
events.description: The Qin ruler who threw open the doors to outside talent, offering land and high office to anyone who could make his backwater state strong. His famous recruitment edict drew Shang Yang west and set Qin's whole rise in motion.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His personal name was Ying Quliang, and he took the throne in 361 BCE at just 21, inheriting a Qin the eastern states still treated as half-barbarian. His "Edict for Seeking Worthy Men" made an unusually blunt promise: bring me a plan to strengthen Qin and I'll give you high rank and share my land with you. He backed Shang Yang to the hilt for over twenty years despite furious opposition from Qin's old families, and in 350 BCE he moved the capital to a brand-new planned city, Xianyang, which would remain Qin's seat right up through the First Emperor. The moment Duke Xiao died in 338 BCE, the nobles he'd held in check moved to destroy Shang Yang.

events.label: Shang Yang's Legalist Reforms
events.description: The most radical overhaul any Chinese state had ever attempted. Shang Yang gutted the hereditary nobility, made military rank something you earned by killing, knit households into spy-on-your-neighbor groups, and swapped feudal fiefs for crown-run counties.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He rolled out the reforms in two waves, the first around 356 BCE and a second around 350 BCE when the capital moved to the new city of Xianyang on the Wei River. The system of earned ranks had twenty levels, each tied to land, servants, and tax breaks, and a soldier's promotion was measured literally in the count of enemy heads he brought back. Shang Yang also pushed families to split up: households with two or more grown sons living together paid double tax, a deliberate nudge to break up big clans into small taxpaying, soldier-producing units the state could track. The whole apparatus survived his execution because the people who now held power owed it to his ladder, not to bloodline.

events.label: King Huiwen of Qin
events.description: The Qin ruler who executed Shang Yang but kept every one of his reforms. King Huiwen eliminated the reformer who had humiliated his tutor when he was crown prince, then continued building the Legalist state Shang Yang had designed.

details.label: Revenge and Pragmatism
details.text: As crown prince, King Huiwen had been punished under Shang Yang's laws (his tutor's nose was cut off for the prince's offense). When he took the throne, he had Shang Yang executed — but recognized that the reforms were too effective to reverse.

details.label: Expansion
details.text: Under Huiwen, Qin conquered the Sichuan Basin and began the aggressive eastern expansion that would culminate in unification a century later.

details.label: Significance
details.text: The fact that Shang Yang's personal enemy kept his system intact proved the reforms had become self-sustaining — they no longer depended on any individual.

events.label: Bai Qi
events.description: Qin's most feared general, a commander who reportedly never lost a battle and earned the nickname "the human butcher." His mass execution of Zhao's surrendered army at Changping made his name a byword for both genius and atrocity.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Records of the Grand Historian credits him with taking more than 70 cities across his thirty-plus years of command and never recording a single defeat, with later tradition tallying the dead he was responsible for at over a million, hence the grim nickname Ren Tu, "human butcher." His downfall came after Changping: he refused to lead the follow-up siege of Zhao's capital Handan, arguing it couldn't be won, and his rival the chancellor Fan Ju whispered that a sulking, all-powerful general was a danger. The king stripped Bai Qi of his titles, drove him from Xianyang, and in 257 BCE sent him a sword at a place called Duyou with the order to kill himself, which he did.

events.label: Conquest of the Sichuan Basin
events.description: Qin's annexation of the rich Sichuan basin to the southwest, which handed the state a whole second breadbasket. The grain it produced, later supercharged by irrigation, would feed the armies that swallowed the six rival kingdoms.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The conquest in 316 BCE settled a famous strategy debate at the Qin court: the advisor Zhang Yi wanted to strike east into the heartland of the central plains first, while the general Sima Cuo argued for grabbing the soft, wealthy southern states of Shu and Ba instead. King Huiwen sided with Sima Cuo, reasoning that taking Shu would add land, grain, and manpower without provoking a grand coalition of the eastern states, and the gamble paid off enormously. The basin became Qin's engine room, so productive that historians have likened it to the state's fuel reactor, and unlike an eastern war it cost Qin almost no diplomatic backlash.

events.label: Han Feizi
events.description: A prince of the small state of Han and the writer who gave Legalism (rule by hard law, reward, and punishment rather than virtue) its sharpest, most complete philosophical voice. His essays so dazzled Ying Zheng that the king said he'd die happy just to meet the author.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He reportedly had a bad stammer, so he poured his arguments onto the page instead of debating aloud, leaving a 55-chapter book (the Han Feizi) that is also one of the richest surviving sources of Warring States anecdotes. He had studied alongside Li Si under the Confucian master Xunzi, which made it doubly cruel that when Han sent him to Qin as an envoy around 233 BCE, Li Si had him jailed and pressured him into swallowing poison rather than risk being outshone. The irony runs deep: a Confucian's two star pupils became the masterminds of the empire that would later try to stamp Confucianism out.

events.label: Battle of Changping
events.description: The bloodiest battle of the Warring States, and the one that doomed Zhao. After a years-long standoff, Qin tricked Zhao into swapping its cautious veteran for an aggressive rookie, who marched straight into a trap. The surrendered Zhao army was then slaughtered en masse.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The killing blow wasn't really the fighting, it was the siege after: Bai Qi cut the Zhao army off from food for forty-six days before it surrendered. The battlefield sits near modern Gaoping in Shanxi province, and farmers there have turned up human bones for centuries; a pit excavated in the 1990s held layers of skeletons, many with signs of violent death, lending hard physical weight to the ancient massacre accounts. The famous 400,000 figure comes from the Han historian Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, written roughly a century and a half later, and many modern historians treat it as an upper-bound estimate rather than a head count. The defeat broke Zhao's ability to field a great army and left Qin's eventual conquest of all China only a matter of time.

events.label: Qin Shi Huang (Ying Zheng)
events.description: Born Ying Zheng around 259 BCE, the boy-king of Qin grew into the man who conquered all of China and crowned himself its First Emperor. Ruthless, tireless, and obsessed with control (and, late in life, with cheating death), he built the imperial system that ran China for the next two thousand years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He was born in Handan, the enemy Zhao capital, where his father was living as a political hostage; when Qin armies besieged the city around 257 BCE, his father fled and left the toddler and his mother behind to survive under hostile guard for years. He died on the road in July 210 BCE during a grand tour of the east, reportedly while chasing elixirs of immortality peddled by court alchemists. The English word "China" descends from "Qin" (pronounced "chin"), and so do the Persian "Chin" and the Sanskrit "Cina."

events.label: Liu Bang
events.description: A peasant-born minor lawman from Pei County who outmaneuvered the aristocratic warlord Xiang Yu, founded the Han dynasty in 202 BCE, and ruled as its first emperor. He kept the Qin's machinery of state while throwing out the cruelty that had sunk it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The whole Han dynasty, and the word "Han" that most Chinese people use for themselves today, traces back to a consolation prize: after the Qin fell in 206 BCE, Xiang Yu shoved Liu Bang off to the poor, remote backcountry of Hanzhong (south of the Qinling mountains) with the throwaway title "King of Han." He turned it into a dynasty. Legend says Liu Bang once sliced a giant snake in half on a country road, and a wailing old woman declared it was her son, the child of the White Emperor, killed by the son of the Red Emperor — a tidy origin myth marking him as heaven's pick. He also nearly died at the Hongmen Banquet (206 BCE), a dinner Xiang Yu set up to have him assassinated; Liu Bang faked being drunk and slipped out alive.

events.label: Li Mu of Zhao
events.description: Zhao's last great general and the one man whose battlefield skill kept Qin out. Twice he beat back Qin invasions, so Qin gave up trying to defeat him in the field and instead bribed Zhao's own court into having him killed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Li Mu first made his name on the northern frontier against the Xiongnu nomads, where he spent years feigning timidity, refusing battle until the raiders grew contemptuous, then sprang a massive encirclement that reportedly destroyed a force of well over a hundred thousand. Against Qin he was just as deadly: in 233 BCE he smashed a Qin army at Fei, a victory that won him the noble title "Lord Wu'an." When the general Wang Jian's invasion stalled against him, Qin agents bribed the corrupt Zhao courtier Guo Kai to spread the lie that Li Mu was plotting rebellion. The Zhao king fell for it and had him removed and killed around 229 BCE; within a year the capital fell and Zhao ceased to exist.

events.label: Wang Jian
events.description: Qin's shrewdest old general, the man who took Chu when no one else could. When the king lowballed the troop numbers, Wang Jian insisted on 600,000 or nothing, was proven right when the smaller army was smashed, then won by waiting out the enemy for a full year.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Commanding nearly Qin's entire army made Wang Jian dangerous in the king's eyes, so he played it safe by repeatedly begging Ying Zheng for fields, houses, and gardens, deliberately looking greedy to prove he had no designs on the throne. The tactic was the whole point: a general obsessed with real estate is a general the king need not fear. Both his son Wang Ben and grandson Wang Li became Qin commanders, making the family one of the dynasty's great military houses.

events.label: Lü Buwei
events.description: Lü Buwei was a merchant prince who bankrolled Ying Zheng's father to the Qin throne and became chancellor. He compiled the encyclopedic Lüshi Chunqiu and wielded near-absolute power — until the young king came of age and forced him out.

details.label: Who He Was
details.text: A wealthy Wei merchant who saw political investment as the ultimate business. He helped a minor Qin prince named Zichu become king, becoming chancellor as his reward. Ancient sources sometimes claimed he was Ying Zheng's biological father — likely scandalous propaganda.

details.label: His Intellectual Project
details.text: Lü Buwei sponsored thousands of scholars to compile the Lüshi Chunqiu — an eclectic encyclopedia of philosophy, history, and statecraft. He hung a copy from the city gate with 1,000 gold coins, challenging anyone to change a single word.

details.label: His Fall
details.text: When Ying Zheng came of age, Lü Buwei's influence became politically toxic. The king stripped him of his title and later ordered him to relocate far from court. He drank poison rather than comply.

events.label: Li Si
events.description: Li Si was the chief minister who turned Qin's conquest into a lasting machine of government. He pushed the standardization of script, law, and measures that knit China together, argued down the old feudal nobility, and ran the empire's bureaucracy for some three decades.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He came up from nothing in Chu, where he started as a lowly clerk; legend says watching rats grow fat in a granary while their cousins starved in the latrine convinced him that a man's fate is just a matter of which place he lands in. After the First Emperor died, Li Si helped the eunuch Zhao Gao forge the succession and put the weak prince Hu Hai on the throne, a deal that backfired spectacularly. In 208 BCE Zhao Gao turned on him: Li Si was tortured into a false confession and executed by being cut in half at the waist in the Xianyang marketplace, his entire clan wiped out alongside him.

events.label: Ying Zheng Becomes King of Qin
events.description: The future Qin Shi Huang ascended to the Qin throne at thirteen when his father died unexpectedly. Born Ying Zheng, the boy king spent his first decade surviving court intrigues before he could begin his conquests.

details.label: An Unpromising Start
details.text: The future Qin Shi Huang was born in Handan while his father was a hostage of Zhao. His father's return to Qin and rapid rise to the throne was engineered by the merchant Lü Buwei, who served as regent during the boy king's minority.

details.label: Palace Intrigues
details.text: The years 246–238 BCE were marked by palace factions. Lü Buwei wielded enormous power. A court scandal involving Lao Ai — a man Lü Buwei introduced to the queen mother — ended in open rebellion, which Ying Zheng crushed in 238 BCE.

details.label: Coming Into His Own
details.text: After exiling Lü Buwei and executing Lao Ai, the 21-year-old king personally took control of Qin's government. He assembled advisors including Li Si and began planning the conquest of the remaining states.

events.label: Zheng Guo Canal
events.description: A massive irrigation canal across the Guanzhong plain, secretly meant to bankrupt Qin with overwork. The plot backfired spectacularly: the canal turned barren land into farmland and helped pay for the very conquests it was supposed to prevent.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The canal ran from a head intake at Hukou on the Jing River eastward to the Luo River, a main channel of roughly 93 miles (150 km), and was named for the Han spy-engineer who designed it, Zheng Guo. Its clever trick was using the Jing's silt-heavy water on purpose: the mud-laden flow both watered and fertilized the region's salty, alkaline soil, reclaiming land that had grown nothing. Records claim it brought roughly 40,000 qing (about 267,000 hectares) into cultivation with yields so reliable that Guanzhong, the old saying went, no longer knew famine years. When the spy plot was exposed mid-build, Zheng Guo's defense, that the canal would genuinely enrich Qin, was so obviously true the king let him finish it.

events.label: Meng Tian
events.description: Meng Tian was the First Emperor's most trusted general, the man who drove the Xiongnu out of the Ordos and oversaw both the Great Wall and the Straight Road. He guarded the northern frontier alongside Crown Prince Fusu, which made him a marked man the moment the emperor died.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Meng Tian came from a military dynasty — his grandfather and father had both been Qin generals before him. Tradition also credits him with perfecting the Chinese writing brush (the soft, ink-loaded brush of Chinese calligraphy), and the town of Huzhou still honors him as the founder of its famous brush-making craft, though historians doubt he truly invented it. When the emperor died, the eunuch Zhao Gao forged an order commanding both Fusu and Meng Tian to kill themselves; Meng Tian commanded 300,000 troops and could have rebelled, but he swallowed poison instead, and Zhao Gao wiped out his whole family.

events.label: Terracotta Army
events.description: A buried army of more than 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers — every face unique — set in battle formation to guard the First Emperor in the afterlife. Lost for over two thousand years until farmers digging a well stumbled onto it in 1974.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Despite fifty years of digging, only about a quarter of the figures have actually been lifted out of the ground. Pit 1 alone — the size of two soccer fields — is thought to hold over 6,000 warriors and horses plus more than 50 chariots, split between eleven earthen corridors, and most of them are still down there. Every figure was assembled like a kit from mass-produced parts (legs, torsos, arms, heads), then hand-finished to make it one of a kind, so the workshops got both factory speed and individual faces.

events.label: First Emperor's Mausoleum Complex
events.description: An entire underground world — nearly 200 pits, tombs, and buildings spread across roughly 22 square miles (57 sq km) — built for the First Emperor over 36 years. The Terracotta Army is just the eastern guard; the burial mound itself sits sealed and unexcavated at the center.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It is the largest mausoleum complex on Earth, and the warriors are only a sliver of it: archaeologists have turned up half-scale bronze chariots with gold and silver fittings, a pit of stone armor laced from hundreds of limestone plates, real horse skeletons, and even bronze cranes and swans posed beside a fake river. One pit (catalogued K9801) tops 13,000 square meters on its own. UNESCO listed the whole site in 1987, and the central tomb chamber holding the coffin has never been opened.

events.label: Lushi Chunqiu (Annals of Lu Buwei)
events.description: A sprawling encyclopedia of philosophy, history, and statecraft, compiled around 239 BCE by an army of scholars working under the merchant-minister Lü Buwei. He reportedly hung a copy at the Xianyang gate with 1,000 gold pieces promised to anyone who could improve a single word. Nobody claimed it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The stunt gave Chinese a lasting idiom — yi zi qian jin, "one word worth a thousand gold" — still used today for writing of supreme value. The book itself was deliberately huge and orderly: more than 200,000 words arranged into 12 "Almanacs," 8 "Examinations," and 6 "Discourses," a structure meant to mirror a complete cosmos. Rather than push one school, it tried to blend the best of all of them into a governing blueprint — the exact eclectic, free-thinking spirit that the First Emperor's book-burning would later try to stamp out.

events.label: Lao Ai Rebellion
events.description: The palace scandal that nearly toppled Ying Zheng before he could rule. Lao Ai, a court favorite who had secretly fathered two sons with the king's own mother, grabbed the royal seals and raised troops in 238 BCE just as the king was coming of age. The rebellion collapsed within days.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Lao Ai had been smuggled into the queen mother's household disguised as a castrated palace servant, a fraud arranged (according to the historian Sima Qian) by the chancellor Lü Buwei to get himself out of the affair. He had been showered with land and the title Marquis of Changxin, and even gave himself the brazen nickname "false father" of the king. Ying Zheng's revenge was total: Lao Ai was torn apart between chariots, three generations of his relatives were killed, and the two young half-brothers were reportedly beaten to death in sacks.

events.label: Expulsion Order and Li Si's Remonstrance
events.description: After discovering Zheng Guo was a spy, Ying Zheng's advisors pushed an order expelling all foreign-born officials from Qin. Li Si, himself a foreigner from Chu, wrote a famous remonstrance arguing that Qin's strength depended on absorbing talent from everywhere. The order was reversed.

details.label: The Crisis
details.text: The discovery that the engineer Zheng Guo was a Han spy triggered xenophobic panic at the Qin court. An edict ordered all foreign-born officials to leave Qin — which would have gutted the administration, since Qin had recruited talent from every state.

details.label: Li Si's Argument
details.text: Li Si's remonstrance became one of the most celebrated essays in Chinese political literature. He catalogued every foreign-born figure who had made Qin great — from Shang Yang to music and jewels — arguing that Qin's openness to talent was its greatest advantage.

details.label: Outcome
details.text: Ying Zheng reversed the expulsion order. Li Si's remonstrance saved his own career and preserved Qin's meritocratic culture. The episode demonstrated how close Qin came to sabotaging itself through nativism.

events.label: Xiang Yu
events.description: The towering warrior of the anti-Qin revolt: grandson of a Chu general killed by Qin, said to be strong enough to lift a bronze cauldron, and undefeated in major battle until the very end. He fought to restore the old aristocratic order — and that rigidity destroyed him.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Born in 232 BCE, he was only about 30 when he died in 202 BCE. On his last night, trapped at Gaixia, he is said to have composed a farewell poem (the "Song of Gaixia") while his beloved Consort Yu killed herself — a scene that became the basis for the famous Peking opera "Farewell My Concubine." Cornered at the Wujiang River and offered a boat to escape, he refused out of shame at how many of his hometown soldiers had died, fought one last stand on foot, and cut his own throat.

events.label: Han Xin
events.description: Liu Bang's military genius — a commander whose campaigns dismantled Xiang Yu's allies one by one and drove him into the final trap at Gaixia. Widely ranked among the greatest strategists China ever produced.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His signature trick was the "back to the river" formation: at the Battle of Jingxing he deliberately pinned his outnumbered men against a river so retreat was impossible, then crushed a Zhao army several times his size — a maneuver still taught as a textbook example. He'd come up from nothing, once so poor a washerwoman pitied him and fed him, and as a youth he swallowed the humiliation of crawling between a bully's legs rather than fight. His reward for winning the empire was grim: in 196 BCE Liu Bang's wife, Empress Lü, had him lured into a palace and executed on suspicion of plotting rebellion.

events.label: Conquest of Han
events.description: The opening move of Qin's nine-year war to swallow the six rival kingdoms. Han was the weakest and was picked to fall first for easy momentum: the general Nei Shi Teng overran it in a single campaign and captured its king in 230 BCE.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Qin had been gnawing at Han for decades, so by 230 BCE it was already battered and nearly defenseless. The captured King An was spared at first, but when Han loyalists rose in revolt in the old capital the next year, Qin crushed them and had him executed. Han's lands were reorganized into Qin's new Yingchuan Commandery, the first piece of the centralized, governor-run system that would eventually cover all of China.

events.label: Conquest of Zhao
events.description: The grudge conquest. Zhao had bloodied Qin before, so when its brilliant general Li Mu kept repelling invasions, Qin simply bribed the Zhao court into executing its own best commander. With Li Mu gone, the kingdom fell fast and its capital was taken in 228 BCE.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Handan, the captured Zhao capital, was the very city where Ying Zheng had been born and spent a frightened childhood as a hostage; the historian Sima Qian says he came back to personally settle scores with the families who had tormented his mother and him. The kill-Li-Mu trick worked through a bribed minister who poisoned the king's mind against the general, who was then arrested and put to death on trumped-up charges. A surviving Zhao prince fled north and declared himself "King of Dai," holding out a remnant kingdom until Qin finally snuffed it in 222 BCE.

events.label: Jing Ke's Assassination Attempt
events.description: The most famous near-miss in Chinese history. In 227 BCE the kingdom of Yan sent the swordsman Jing Ke to murder the king of Qin, hiding a poisoned dagger inside a rolled-up map. The king dodged, drew his sword, and cut the assassin down, then sped up his invasion out of fury.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: To get close, Jing Ke carried the severed head of Fan Yuqi, a Qin defector who volunteered his own death for the cause, along with the map. His teenage backup, a hitman named Qin Wuyang who had supposedly killed his first man at thirteen, lost his nerve and froze at the palace steps. The plot gave Chinese the lasting idiom "the map unrolls and the dagger appears" for a scheme exposed at the last second, and Jing Ke's farewell at the freezing Yi River, where he sang of the brave man who departs never to return, made him a tragic hero retold for over two thousand years.

events.label: Conquest of Wei
events.description: The siege Qin won with water. Wei's capital Daliang sat behind walls and moats too strong to storm, so the general Wang Ben diverted nearby rivers to drown it. After three months underwater the walls gave way and the king surrendered in 225 BCE.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Daliang sat at the junction of several waterways with a wide moat and drawbridged gates, which is exactly why Wang Ben turned that water against it, channeling the Yellow River and the Hong Canal into the city for three months. Ancient accounts say the flooding killed roughly a hundred thousand people, soldiers and civilians alike, a deliberate atrocity meant as a warning to every kingdom still standing. The drowned city is today's Kaifeng, in Henan, which later became one of the largest cities on Earth as a Song-dynasty capital.

events.label: Conquest of Chu
events.description: Qin's hardest fight. Chu was the vast, rich southern kingdom, and the first invasion under the young general Li Xin was routed. Only Wang Jian's full 600,000-man army, after a patient year-long standoff, finally broke Chu in 223 BCE.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Wang Jian camped his huge force for a year, letting his men rest and play games while the impatient Chu army wore itself out, then struck the moment the enemy turned to leave. The last Chu general, Xiang Yan, is said to have cut his own throat cursing Qin as he died. The grudge outlived the kingdom: tradition makes Xiang Yan the grandfather of Xiang Yu, the warlord who less than two decades later helped topple the Qin dynasty and burned its capital to the ground.

events.label: Conquest of Yan and Qi
events.description: The last two kingdoms fall. Yan was finished off in 222 BCE after its desperate king killed his own son and sent the head to Qin to beg for peace. Qi, which had bribed itself into neutrality, simply surrendered in 221 BCE without a battle and trusted Qin's empty promises.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Yan's King Xi murdered his heir, Prince Dan (the very man who had sent Jing Ke after the Qin king), and shipped the severed head south as an apology; Qin pocketed the head and conquered Yan anyway. Qi's chancellor Hou Sheng had spent years on Qin's payroll, talking the Qi court out of helping the other states as they were picked off one by one. When Qin finally turned east, Qi stood alone and folded; its surrendered king was reportedly banished to a wooded patch and left to starve, mocked in a folk ballad as the king "made to die in a common village."

events.label: Declaration of Empire
events.description: In 221 BCE the Qin king Ying Zheng invented a brand-new royal title, huangdi ("emperor"), abolished the old feudal kingdoms, and carved his conquered realm into 36 commanderies (provinces) run by officials he appointed and could fire.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He stitched the new word huangdi together from two pieces of deep mythology: huang from the legendary Three Sovereigns and di from the Five Emperors, demigod founders of Chinese prehistory — so the title literally borrowed the prestige of gods. To make the throne's authority touchable, he had a famous chunk of jade called the Heshibi carved into the Heirloom Seal of the Realm, a physical stamp meant to prove who held the Mandate of Heaven; it got handed down emperor to emperor for over a thousand years before vanishing in the 10th century. Abolishing feudalism in favor of the commandery system was the policy of his prime minister Li Si, designed specifically so the chaos of the Warring States could never come back.

events.label: Qin Uniform Legal Code
events.description: Qin pushed its Legalist law code — refined over a century since Shang Yang — across the whole empire, so that for the first time one written, publicly posted body of law governed all of China instead of a thousand local customs and aristocratic whims.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Most of what we actually know about this code comes from one man's grave — a minor official named Xi whose tomb gave up over a thousand bamboo law strips (the Shuihudi find). They show a state obsessed with paperwork: there were statutes on how much grain a granary could lose to rats before someone was held responsible, and step-by-step forensic manuals for investigating a death — measure the wounds, log the scene, interview the neighbors. The collective-punishment principle was real and brutal: under the "mutual responsibility" system that Shang Yang had set up, neighbors were bound into groups and a household could be dragged down for failing to report a crime next door.

events.label: Qin Calendar Reform
events.description: Qin imposed one calendar on the empire, the Zhuanxu system, which started each year in the tenth month instead of the traditional first — fixing the chaos of six kingdoms whose years didn't even begin on the same day. A shared calendar meant taxes, conscription, and court business could finally be coordinated.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The calendar got tangled up in the emperor's own name. His given name was Zheng, which sounds exactly like Zhengyue, the word for the first month — and you were not allowed to write or say a ruler's name. So the first month was quietly renamed Duanyue (the "upright" or "proper" month) to dodge the taboo, with real legal penalties for getting it wrong. The tenth-month new year didn't stick: the Han threw it out and moved the new year back to spring, where it has stayed ever since.

events.label: Standardization of Writing
events.description: Li Si scrapped the six kingdoms' rival scripts and imposed one official style — the small seal script (xiaozhuan) — derived from Qin's own writing. For the first time, a scholar at one end of China could read a document written at the other.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: To roll the new script out, the Qin court issued three official primers — Li Si's own Cangjiepian (a wordbook of roughly 3,300 characters), the Yuanlipian by the eunuch Zhao Gao, and the Boxuepian by Humu Jing — the ancient equivalent of a national style guide for scribes. The irony is that the elegant, curvy seal script was a pain to write quickly, so working clerks were already cutting corners with a faster, blockier hand called clerical script (lishu), and it's that everyday shortcut, not Li Si's showpiece, that the modern Chinese character is actually descended from.

events.label: Standardization of Weights, Measures & Currency
events.description: Qin junked the knife coins, spade coins, and cowrie shells of the conquered states and made one money for everyone: the round bronze ban liang ("half-tael") with a square hole punched in the middle. The design would outlive the dynasty by two thousand years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The name was a promise printed on the coin itself: "ban liang" means half a tael, and the coin was meant to weigh exactly that — roughly a quarter-ounce (about 7 grams), around 1.25 inches (32 mm) across. The square hole wasn't just symbolism (round Heaven, square Earth); it was a factory trick — coins came off the casting mold rough, so workers threaded a batch onto a square rod and filed all the edges at once, which a round hole would have let spin uselessly. The very last Chinese coins to keep this round-with-a-square-hole shape were minted under the Qing, the dynasty that fell in 1912.

events.label: Axle Width Standardization
events.description: Qin fixed a single legal width for every cart axle in the empire. Until then, carts from different kingdoms cut different-width grooves into the dirt roads, so a wagon built in one region literally couldn't ride the ruts of another — standardizing the gauge made the whole road network usable by everyone.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The reform was famous enough to become a slogan — "carts on the same track, writing in the same script" — paired forever with the script reform as the twin symbols of a unified China. The historian Sima Qian, writing under the Han a century or so later, lists the standard axle width right alongside coins, weights, and measures in his account of what the First Emperor unified. It's a strikingly modern idea: like railway gauge in the 1800s, agreeing on one width turned thousands of miles of disconnected local tracks into a single working network.

events.label: Qin Crossbow Mass Production
events.description: The crossbow trigger — the small bronze mechanism that holds and releases the string — was made by the Qin in standardized, swappable batches, so a broken one could be replaced from stock. It's some of the earliest evidence anywhere of parts built to a common specification.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Researchers studying the Terracotta Army's triggers found they weren't quite the flawless interchangeable parts of a modern factory: pieces were cast in small batches from shared molds, then filed and marked by hand so the matching parts could be paired up during assembly. The marks may have noted which worker or mold a piece came from, a way of tracking quality across a sprawling workforce. Even with that hand-fitting, it's a level of organized, repeatable manufacturing the rest of the world wouldn't match for a very long time.

events.label: Commandery-County System
events.description: Instead of handing conquered land to relatives as feudal lords, Qin split the empire into 36 commanderies (later more), each carved into counties and run by appointed officials who could be promoted, moved, or fired at will. Nobody inherited a job; the bureaucracy ran on obedience, not bloodline.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The system came out of a real argument at court: the chancellor Wang Wan urged the emperor to make his sons regional kings the way the old Zhou had done, and Li Si shot it down — that, he said, was exactly the mistake that had bred centuries of war. To make sure no commandery boss could go rogue, each was run by a built-in three-way check: a civil governor, a separate military commander, and an imperial inspector watching both of them. Underneath the 36 commanderies sat close to a thousand counties, a skeleton of administration so sound that every later dynasty kept the basic shape.

events.label: Five Phases State Cosmology
events.description: Qin made the Five Phases (wuxing) — the cycle of Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water thought to drive everything from the seasons to the rise and fall of dynasties — its official ideology, claiming the Water phase for itself. Water was tied to the color black and the number six, so Qin draped its court in black and built rituals around sixes.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The logic was a cosmic power grab: in the cycle, Water overcomes Fire, and the previous Zhou dynasty had ruled under Fire — so Qin's victory wasn't just military, it was the universe turning its wheel. The number six ran deep into policy: official caps and carriages were measured in sixes, and the empire was first cut into 36 commanderies (six times six). Water's other association was cold, hidden severity, which Qin's thinkers took as heavenly endorsement of harsh, unbending law — the cosmos itself, they argued, told them to rule without mercy.

events.label: Great Wall Construction
events.description: Between roughly 215 and 210 BCE, General Meng Tian stitched the old frontier walls of Qin, Zhao, and Yan into one rammed-earth barrier running thousands of miles along the empire's northern edge to wall out the Xiongnu nomads. It was a chain of beacon towers, garrisons, and packed dirt — not the stone postcard most people picture.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Qin wall ran from Lintao in the far west to Liaodong near the sea, but almost none of it survives — what you see in tourist photos is a Ming-dynasty rebuild from over 1,500 years later, in stone and brick. Meng Tian didn't just build a wall; he resettled tens of thousands of colonists into the reclaimed Ordos loop (the "Hetao" region inside the Yellow River's northern bend) to farm it and feed his 300,000-strong army on the spot. The construction earned the wall its grim nickname as "the longest cemetery on Earth," and archaeologists really have turned up mass graves of laborers along its route.

events.label: Imperial Inspection Tours
events.description: Qin Shi Huang made six major inspection tours across his empire, erecting stone steles inscribed with his achievements at sacred mountains and on the seacoast. The tours served to legitimize his authority, inspect local administration, and search for immortality.

details.label: Performance of Power
details.text: The imperial procession — thousands of soldiers, courtiers, and officials crossing the empire — was itself a form of governance. It showed the emperor's face to populations who might never otherwise see him, and gave local officials reason to maintain order.

details.label: The Stele Inscriptions
details.text: Li Si composed inscriptions for steles erected on Mount Tai, Mount Langya, and Mount Jieshi on the eastern coast. The texts proclaimed the emperor's achievements in prose so formal it was almost incomprehensible — deliberately intimidating rather than informative.

details.label: The Fatal Fifth Tour
details.text: On his fifth inspection tour in 210 BCE, the emperor fell seriously ill near the coast. He died on the road — his body was transported to Xianyang in secrecy to prevent premature power struggles, with fish carts placed near his wagon to mask the smell of decomposition.

events.label: Qin Road Network (Chidao)
events.description: Starting around 220 BCE, the First Emperor laced the empire together with engineered imperial highways radiating from the capital Xianyang — graded, drained, tree-lined, and wide enough for chariots to ride six abreast. Roads moved goods, but more importantly they moved armies fast.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The most spectacular piece was a separate north-south military road, the Zhidao or "Straight Road," begun around 212 BCE: General Meng Tian drove it roughly 435 miles (700 km) almost dead straight from near Xianyang up to the northern frontier at Jiuyuan (near modern Baotou) so troops could rush to meet the nomadic Xiongnu raiders. Archaeologists still find stretches of it today, and some excavated sections run an astonishing 200 feet (around 60 m) wide — comparable to a modern multi-lane motorway. The Han kept every mile Qin had built and simply added more.

events.label: Quest for Immortality
events.description: The most coldly rational ruler in the ancient world spent his final decade chasing eternal life — funding alchemists, climbing sacred mountains to sacrifice, dispatching fleets to mythical islands, and swallowing pills laced with mercury that his magicians swore would make him immortal.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The remedy almost certainly killed him: the First Emperor died in 210 BCE at just 49, and many scholars blame chronic mercury poisoning from his own elixirs. He took the obsession to the grave literally — Sima Qian wrote that his tomb held the rivers and seas of China recreated in flowing mercury beneath a jeweled map of the heavens. The tomb has never been excavated, but modern soil tests around the mound near Xi'an still register mercury readings far above the natural background, lending the ancient account eerie credibility.

events.label: Imperial Stele Inscriptions
events.description: Li Si composed formal inscriptions for stone steles erected during the First Emperor's inspection tours at Mount Tai, Mount Langya, and Mount Jieshi. Written in the new standardized small seal script, they proclaimed the emperor's achievements in deliberately intimidating prose.

details.label: Style
details.text: The stele inscriptions were written in four-character verse so formal it was almost incomprehensible to common readers — deliberately intimidating rather than informative. They proclaimed the emperor's unification, his virtue, and the end of the Warring States chaos.

details.label: Calligraphic Significance
details.text: As the first major public texts written in the new small seal script, the steles served as models for the standardized writing system across the empire.

details.label: Survival
details.text: Most original steles have been lost or eroded, but their texts were preserved in Sima Qian's Shiji, providing firsthand examples of Qin imperial rhetoric.

events.label: Feng and Shan Sacrifices on Mount Tai
events.description: In 219 BCE the First Emperor climbed Mount Tai, holiest of China's five sacred peaks, to perform the feng and shan rites — ceremonies announcing a ruler so accomplished that Heaven itself endorsed him. When Confucian scholars questioned whether he qualified, he waved them off and did it anyway.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ceremony was so rarefied that across two thousand years of Chinese history only a handful of emperors ever dared attempt it. Tradition holds that a sudden storm caught Qin Shi Huang on the mountain, and he sheltered under a pine tree — which he then rewarded with a noble rank, the kind of imperial whim that delighted later storytellers. He also left behind a stone stele carved with his achievements, part of a habit of erecting monuments to himself on his grand tours of the new empire.

events.label: Xu Fu's Maritime Expeditions
events.description: The court alchemist Xu Fu sailed east with 3,000 young men and women to find Penglai, the mythical island of immortals, and bring back the elixir of life. He came back once blaming sea monsters, talked the emperor into bankrolling a bigger fleet, sailed off again, and was never seen in China again.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: That second voyage, around 210 BCE, was no small errand: accounts give it some 60 ships loaded with thousands of crew, the 3,000 children, and craftsmen carrying seeds and tools. Centuries later, Japanese legend claimed Xu Fu simply settled there rather than return empty-handed, and to this day towns like Shingu honor him under his Japanese name, Jofuku, as a bringer of farming, medicine, and silk-making. The historical truth is unprovable, but the shrines and festivals have outlasted the empire he sailed away from by more than two thousand years.

events.label: Ling Canal
events.description: Built roughly 219 to 214 BCE, the Lingqu Canal cut a 21-mile (34 km) channel linking the Xiang River (which drains north to the Yangtze) with the Li River (which drains south to the Pearl), joining China's two greatest river systems for the first time. It let Qin float supplies to its southern armies instead of hauling them over mountains.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The canal is the oldest contour transport canal in the world, designed by an engineer named Shi Lu, and its plowshare-shaped splitting weir (the "Huazui") still divides the Xiang's water between the two basins today. A staircase of roughly 36 sluice gates managed the water levels, an early ancestor of the modern canal lock. Once finished, it opened a continuous inland waterway of about 1,200 miles (2,000 km) from north China down to the Pearl River delta — and 2,200 years on, it still carries water and is a recognized cultural heritage site.

events.label: Shuihudi Bamboo Texts
events.description: In 1975, archaeologists opened a tomb at Shuihudi in Hubei and found the working law library of a Qin county official named Xi — bamboo strips covered in legal codes, official forms, and how-to guides. It's the closest thing we have to a Qin bureaucrat's actual desk drawer.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The haul was found in December 1975 in Tomb No. 11 at Shuihudi, Yunmeng County: 1,155 bamboo strips carrying nearly 40,000 characters, many of them packed in around the body itself. They were a genuine first — before this, almost no actual Qin legal text survived, so historians had been stuck reading later writers' descriptions of a system everyone agreed was monstrous. Among the documents are Xi's own brief life records, which let scholars work out that he was born around 262 BCE and died around 217 BCE, still on the job.

events.label: Southern Campaigns Against the Baiyue
events.description: Around 214 BCE Qin pushed south to conquer the Baiyue (the "Hundred Yue," the many non-Chinese peoples of what is now Guangdong, Guangxi, and northern Vietnam). The jungle terrain forced Qin to dig the Lingqu Canal just to keep its armies fed, and victory pulled the far south into the Chinese world for good.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: One ancient source claims a staggering 500,000 troops in five separate armies were thrown at the campaign, though that figure comes from a philosophy book and may be inflated. The fighting was brutal: the Yue melted into the forests and ambushed the invaders, and the overall commander, a general named Tu Sui, was killed in battle. After the conquest one of Qin's frontier officers, Zhao Tuo, was left in charge of the south — and when the dynasty collapsed he broke away to found his own independent kingdom, Nanyue, ruling it for decades.

events.label: Burning of Books
events.description: On Li Si's advice, the First Emperor ordered every privately held book of poetry, history, and philosophy burned, sparing only manuals on farming, medicine, and divination plus Qin's own records. Talking about the banned texts to criticize the state was a capital crime.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Anyone who failed to hand over forbidden books within thirty days wasn't just fined — they were branded and shipped north as convict labor on the Great Wall. The ban worked less well than Li Si hoped: a scholar named Fu Sheng bricked a copy of the Book of History into the wall of his house, and when the Han dynasty came digging it back out, he could still recite 28 of its chapters from memory in his nineties. Decades later, more hidden manuscripts reportedly turned up inside a wall of Confucius's old home in his hometown of Qufu.

events.label: Burying of Scholars
events.description: After two court magicians took the emperor's immortality money and bolted, the resulting witch-hunt swept up around 460 scholars, who were executed near the capital. The emperor's eldest son Fusu objected and got himself exiled to the northern frontier — quietly knocking himself out of the line of succession.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Chinese phrase for the whole episode, fenshu kengru, literally means "burn the books and pit the ru" — and historians have argued for centuries over who actually ended up in those pits. Sima Qian's earliest wording points to fangshi (occultists and elixir-peddlers) rather than Confucian scholars; the "Confucian martyrs" version hardened in later retellings. Sima Qian himself was writing under the Han, the dynasty that overthrew Qin and had every reason to paint the First Emperor as a monster.

events.label: Epang Palace
events.description: The First Emperor ordered construction of the massive Epang Palace near Xianyang, intended to be the grandest structure in the empire. The front hall alone was designed to seat 10,000 people. Construction was never completed — halted by the emperor's death and the dynasty's collapse.

details.label: Ambition
details.text: The Epang Palace was planned as the ceremonial heart of the empire. Ancient sources describe the front hall as 500 paces from east to west and 50 feet high, with space for 10,000 people. It would have been the largest wooden structure in the ancient world.

details.label: Never Completed
details.text: Construction began around 212 BCE but was abandoned after the First Emperor's death. The labor demands of the palace, the mausoleum, the Great Wall, and the road network simultaneously pushed Qin's population to the breaking point.

details.label: Archaeological Debate
details.text: Modern archaeology has found the rammed-earth foundation platform but little evidence of the superstructure. The traditional claim that Xiang Yu burned the Epang Palace may be exaggerated — it may never have been completed enough to burn.

events.label: Straight Road (Zhidao)
events.description: Begun in 212 BCE, the Straight Road (Zhidao) was Meng Tian's military superhighway running over 435 miles (700 km) from near the capital Xianyang straight north to the frontier garrison at Jiuyuan, in modern Inner Mongolia. Engineers cut it through mountains and filled valleys to keep it nearly level, so troops could rush north to meet Xiongnu raids.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It's been called the world's first true expressway: averaging around 130 feet (40 m) wide and widening to nearly 200 feet (60 m) in places, broad enough to run several lanes of traffic abreast. The same 300,000-man northern army did the building, racing the road north so fast that crews compacted the roadbed and reinforced its slopes with rammed earth, traces of which archaeologists still dig up. Started in the emperor's lifetime, it wasn't finished until 207 BCE under his weak successor, just as the dynasty was beginning to fall apart.

events.label: Death of Qin Shi Huang
events.description: The First Emperor dropped dead at 49 on the road far from his capital, in the summer of 210 BCE, while touring the eastern coast. He had never named an heir, and the two men at his deathbed forged a succession decree that doomed the dynasty.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He died at the Sand Dune Palace (Shaqiu) in what's now Hebei province, and modern scientists think the mercury-laced "immortality elixirs" his alchemists fed him are a plausible culprit — high mercury levels really have been measured in the soil around his tomb. The body had to be smuggled back to the capital, so officials packed rotting fish around the imperial wagon to mask the stench of decomposition in the summer heat. His tomb near Xi'an is the same complex guarded by the famous Terracotta Army, and it has never been excavated.

events.label: Qin Er Shi (Second Emperor)
events.description: Huhai, a younger son chosen precisely because he was pliable, ruled as Zhao Gao's puppet. He doubled down on his father's brutal labor demands while rebellion spread, until the eunuch he depended on turned on him too.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His reign lasted barely three years, and he died young — accounts put him in his early twenties — forced to take his own life in 207 BCE during a coup Zhao Gao staged at the Wangyi Palace. As a final insult, he was stripped of his imperial title in death and denied an emperor's burial; his modest tomb sits well apart from his father's grand mausoleum near Xi'an. By the time he died, rebel armies were already closing on the capital.

events.label: Zhao Gao
events.description: The palace eunuch who controlled what documents reached the emperor — and used that grip on information to engineer a puppet succession, purge every rival, and run the empire from behind the throne until the last Qin ruler turned the tables on him.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His infamous loyalty test came on a single recorded day in 207 BCE, when he presented a deer to the court and insisted it was a horse; officials who told the truth were quietly killed off later, and the episode gave Chinese a phrase still thrown at propagandists today. His end was poetic: the new ruler Ziying faked an illness, and when Zhao Gao came in person to fetch him for the coronation, an attendant cut him down. His entire clan was then wiped out.

events.label: Mercury Rivers in the Imperial Tomb
events.description: The ancient historian Sima Qian claimed the tomb's interior held flowing rivers and seas of liquid mercury, mimicking China's waterways. Long dismissed as a tall tale — until soil tests in the 1980s found mercury levels far above normal in a pattern that traces the real rivers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mercury vapor is highly toxic, so the contamination may be one practical reason no one has rushed to crack the tomb open. Sima Qian wrote that machines kept the mercury circulating to simulate moving water, and the surveyed hot-spots cluster toward the tomb's northeast and southwest — roughly where China's rivers and the eastern sea would sit on a map. The reading has held up across repeated soil surveys, which is why the mercury detail is now treated as probably true rather than legend.

events.label: Legend of Meng Jiangnü
events.description: The folk tale of Meng Jiangnü, a woman whose grief-stricken weeping over her husband — who died as a conscript building the Great Wall — caused a whole section of the wall to crumble and reveal his bones. It became a lasting popular indictment of the human cost of the First Emperor's ambitions.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The story is counted among China's "Four Great Folktales," alongside the Legend of the White Snake, the Butterfly Lovers, and the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl. Scholars traced its roots back to a bare anecdote in the Zuozhuan chronicle from the Spring and Autumn period (centuries before Qin) about the widow of a warrior named Qi Liang, which storytellers gradually reshaped over the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties into the wall-collapsing legend we know. In other words, the tale that became the wall's most famous protest predates the Qin wall itself by hundreds of years.

events.label: Chen Sheng–Wu Guang Uprising
events.description: Two minor officers escorting 900 conscripts north were stranded by floods past their legal deadline — and since showing up late carried the death penalty, they figured they might as well rebel. Their revolt was the first crack that brought the whole empire down.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: It kicked off at a village called Dazexiang in modern Anhui, and the pair primed their men with fake omens, reportedly stuffing a silk message reading "Chen Sheng will be king" into the belly of a fish and faking a fox's voice crying it in the night. Chen Sheng quickly crowned himself king of a revived "Zhangchu" (Expanded Chu) state. Both men were dead within months — killed by their own followers as the movement fractured — but the historian Sima Qian still gave the lowborn Chen Sheng a chapter normally reserved for nobility, a mark of how much the uprising mattered.

events.label: Battle of Julu
events.description: Xiang Yu shattered the last great Qin field army here in 207 BCE. After crossing the Zhang River to relieve a besieged rebel force, he sank the boats and smashed the cooking pots so his men had no way home — win or starve.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Qin commander Zhang Han surrendered with about 200,000 troops, and Xiang Yu, distrusting so many enemy soldiers and unable to feed them, had nearly all of them buried alive outside the town of Xin'an in Henan — a horror that echoed Qin's own earlier mass killing of Zhao prisoners. The "sink the boats and smash the pots" gamble (po fu chen zhou) became a permanent Chinese expression for burning your bridges and committing totally. Watching rebel generals were reportedly so awed they stayed frozen in their camps rather than join the fight.

events.label: Ziying, Last Ruler of Qin
events.description: The third and final Qin ruler lasted just 46 days. He assassinated the eunuch Zhao Gao by faking illness to lure him in, then surrendered peacefully to Liu Bang — only to be executed weeks later when Xiang Yu arrived and torched the palaces.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tellingly, Ziying never used the title "emperor": with the rebellion swallowing the realm, he downgraded himself to merely "King of Qin," an admission the all-conquering empire was already finished. He surrendered to Liu Bang with a cord around his neck and the imperial seals in hand, the ritual posture of total submission. Liu Bang spared him, but when Xiang Yu marched in he killed Ziying and set fires in the capital that ancient sources claim burned for three months.

events.label: Fall of Xianyang and End of Qin
events.description: Liu Bang's army entered Xianyang in 206 BCE, where the last Qin ruler Ziying surrendered — having killed Zhao Gao only 46 days before. Liu Bang declined to loot the palace or harm the population. When Xiang Yu arrived weeks later, he burned the palaces, looted the treasury, and executed Ziying.

details.label: Two Entrances
details.text: Liu Bang entered Xianyang first, sealed the palace storehouses, withdrew his troops from the city, and posted a notice promising to keep the Qin laws protecting the population. It was masterful political theater — the merciful liberator versus the brutal conqueror.

details.label: Xiang Yu's Destruction
details.text: When Xiang Yu arrived with his larger army, he burned the great Qin palaces — fires reportedly burning for three months. He executed Ziying and divided China among 18 kings, giving Liu Bang a remote western territory deliberately chosen for its isolation.

details.label: The End of an Era
details.text: The Qin dynasty that unified China in 221 BCE was gone by 206 BCE — 15 years of rule. The administrative system, roads, walls, and unified script all survived the dynasty. The Han inherited every institution Qin had created, just without Qin's brutality, and ruled for 400 years.

events.label: Chu-Han Contention
events.description: The four-year civil war that filled the vacuum after Qin fell, pitting Xiang Yu's Western Chu against Liu Bang's Han. The greater warrior won nearly every battle; the better politician won the only war that counted.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Midway through, the exhausted sides actually signed a truce splitting China along the Hong Canal — Chu to the east, Han to the west — a line that survives as the river boundary down the middle of a Chinese chess (xiangqi) board to this day. Liu Bang agreed to it, then tore it up the moment Xiang Yu's army turned its back and marched east. The conflict left a trail of idioms still in everyday use and remains one of the most retold rivalries in Chinese opera, fiction, and film.

events.label: Battle of Gaixia
events.description: The last battle of the Chu-Han war, in 202 BCE. Surrounded and starving, Xiang Yu heard Chu folk songs drifting from the enemy camp and assumed his homeland had already fallen — the moment his army's spirit broke.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Liu Bang's side likely staged the singing on purpose, a psychological blow that gave Chinese the phrase "songs of Chu on all sides" (simian Chuge) for being hopelessly hemmed in by enemies. Xiang Yu burst out of the encirclement with 800 horsemen, but by the time he reached the Wujiang River only a couple dozen were left. When Liu Bang heard of his rival's suicide he reportedly wept and buried him with the honors due a king — a rare gesture toward a defeated enemy.

events.label: Sima Qian
events.description: China's first great historian (roughly 145–86 BCE), whose Records of the Grand Historian (the Shiji) is the main written source for the Qin. Writing about a century after the dynasty fell, he gave us the First Emperor, the tomb, and the mercury rivers.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He paid a brutal price to finish the book. After defending a disgraced general at the court of Emperor Wu of Han, Sima Qian was given a choice between execution and castration; he chose castration — an enormous shame in his culture — specifically so he could live to complete the history his father Sima Tan had started. The finished Shiji ran to around 130 chapters covering some two thousand years, and its biography-driven structure became the template every later Chinese dynastic history copied.

events.label: Yang Zhifa and the 1974 Discovery
events.description: The farmer (often named as the lead among several) who hit terracotta fragments while digging a well during a drought near Xi'an on March 29, 1974 — the strike that uncovered the buried army. He later spent years working at the site museum.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The reward for one of history's greatest finds was tiny: the men were paid 10 yuan per cart of dirt they'd hauled, about 30 yuan total, then roughly a year's wages in a poor rural village. Yang's biggest moment of fame came in 1998, when visiting U.S. president Bill Clinton asked him for his autograph — and Yang, who could barely write his own name, had to practice signing it. He went on to sell warrior replicas in the museum gift shop near the very field where he'd been digging for water.

glossary.definition: A Chinese political philosophy holding that human nature is self-interested and that states are best governed through strict written law, clear rewards and punishments, and centralized power — not moral exhortation. Shang Yang and Han Feizi were its leading practitioners; it was the ideological engine of Qin's rise.

The era from roughly 475 BCE to 221 BCE in which seven major Chinese kingdoms fought for supremacy following the collapse of Zhou central authority. It ended when Qin conquered the other six states. The period also produced the Hundred Schools of Thought.

China's longest dynasty (1046–256 BCE), whose feudal order fragmented into the Warring States. The Zhou introduced the Mandate of Heaven and produced Confucius, Laozi, and Sun Tzu. Qin's unification ended the Zhou era and replaced its feudal model with centralized bureaucratic rule.

The dynasty founded by Liu Bang in 206 BCE that replaced the Qin. The Han ruled for four centuries, explicitly inheriting Qin's administrative institutions (standardized script, roads, bureaucracy) while abandoning Qin's harshest policies. It cemented the imperial Chinese governance model.

The flowering of Chinese philosophy during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, producing Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism, Mohism, and dozens of other schools. The Qin burning of books targeted this intellectual tradition. The Han later reconstructed and institutionalized Confucianism.

The Zhou doctrine that Heaven grants the right to rule to virtuous rulers and withdraws it from the corrupt — signaled by natural disasters, rebellions, and military defeat. Every Chinese dynasty for 3,000 years used this concept to legitimize its rise and explain its predecessor's fall.

A powerful nomadic confederation of the Mongolian steppe that raided Chinese settlements from the 3rd century BCE onward. Qin's Great Wall and northern campaigns under Meng Tian were built primarily to contain Xiongnu incursions. They remained China's principal northern threat through the Han dynasty.

The fertile basin in northwestern China enclosed by mountain ranges, centered on the Wei River. Qin's heartland and the site of its capital Xianyang. The Zheng Guo Canal transformed Guanzhong's alkaline land into productive farmland, directly funding the wars of unification.

The capital of the Qin state and then the Qin Empire, located in the Guanzhong plain near modern Xi'an. The First Emperor built massive palaces here. Xiang Yu burned the city in 206 BCE, destroying the imperial archives and much of the pre-Qin literary record.

China's second-longest river, flowing from the Tibetan plateau through the Loess Plateau to the sea. The cradle of Chinese civilization and the core of the Qin heartland. Qin diverted the Yellow River to flood Wei's capital Daliang during the unification wars.

China's longest river, flowing from the Tibetan plateau to the East China Sea. The Lingqu Canal linked the Yangtze watershed to the Pearl River system, enabling Qin's southern campaigns. The Yangtze valley was Chu territory before conquest.

Capital of the Zhao kingdom, located in modern Hebei. Ying Zheng was born here while his father was held as a diplomatic hostage. Zhao fell when Qin captured Handan in 228 BCE. The emperor reportedly executed officials there who had humiliated him during his childhood.

The most sacred of China's Five Great Mountains, located in Shandong. Performing the feng and shan sacrifices on Mount Tai was reserved for rulers Heaven deemed supremely accomplished. Qin Shi Huang conducted these rites in 219 BCE, asserting his legitimacy as the greatest ruler in history.

The eldest son of Qin Shi Huang, widely regarded as the most capable and humane of the imperial heirs. Exiled to the northern frontier after protesting the execution of scholars in 212 BCE, he was the designated successor. Zhao Gao's forged decree ordered his suicide, which he obeyed out of filial piety.

A major Confucian philosopher (c. 310–235 BCE) whose pessimistic view of human nature — that people require education and ritual to be moral — bridged Confucianism and Legalism. Both Li Si and Han Feizi studied under him, making him the intellectual grandfather of Qin's governing philosophy.

The philosopher (c. 280–233 BCE) who synthesized Legalist thought into its most complete form. His text, the Han Feizi, so impressed Qin Shi Huang that he reportedly said he would die without regret if he could meet its author. Han Feizi came to Qin as a diplomat and died in custody, likely at Li Si's instigation.

The administrative framework Qin imposed across its empire, dividing territory into commanderies (jun) and counties (xian) governed by appointed officials rather than hereditary nobles. Li Si championed it over feudal enfeoffment. This system became the structural basis of Chinese local government for two millennia.

The standardized writing script Li Si created for the Qin Empire in 221 BCE, derived from Qin's own script and used to replace the six different regional scripts of the conquered kingdoms. It is the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters and the foundation of Chinese written unity.

The round bronze coin with a square hole standardized by the Qin as China's universal currency in 221 BCE. The round-coin-with-square-hole design, introduced to replace the six kingdoms' incompatible currencies (knife money, spade money, ring coins), remained China's coin shape through the Qing dynasty — roughly 2,100 years.

The network of imperial highways built by Qin Shi Huang radiating from Xianyang across the empire. Roughly 6,800 km of standardized roads, wide enough for six chariots abreast, with drainage channels, rest stations, and regularly spaced trees. The Han inherited and expanded the entire network.

A Chinese cosmological framework organizing natural phenomena into five categories — Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water — cycling in sequence. Qin associated itself with the Water phase (black, number six), claiming to have superseded the Zhou Fire phase. This framework shaped Qin's calendar, ritual color, and self-presentation.

The most severe category of criminal punishment under ancient Chinese law, involving successive mutilations — tattooing, cutting off the nose, amputation of feet — followed by flogging to death or execution by bisection. Li Si was executed using this method in 208 BCE after Zhao Gao's show trial.

Compulsory unpaid labor required of subjects as a form of taxation, used extensively by the Qin to build the Great Wall, imperial roads, the Ling Canal, and the First Emperor's mausoleum. The brutal conditions and scale of Qin corvée demands were a primary driver of the popular resentment that fueled the 209 BCE rebellions.

The collective term for the non-Chinese peoples inhabiting southern China and Southeast Asia, speaking Austroasiatic and Tai-Kadai languages. Qin launched major campaigns to conquer Baiyue territories, building the Ling Canal to supply those armies. The conquests opened the far south to Chinese settlement.

A court alchemist and magician who Qin Shi Huang twice sent east with fleets and thousands of young men and women to find the mythical Penglai islands and their immortality elixir. He never returned from the second voyage. Later Japanese legends identify him as an early settler — there are shrines to Jofuku in Japan today.

Mythical islands in the eastern sea where Chinese tradition held that immortals lived and possessed the elixir of life. Qin Shi Huang's obsessive quest for immortality led him to send maritime expeditions to find Penglai. The islands remained a recurring motif in Chinese literature and Daoist mythology.

China's first great historian (c. 145–86 BCE), author of the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), the primary ancient source for Qin dynasty history. Writing a century after the Qin's fall, Sima Qian compiled court records, oral traditions, and official documents into the model for all subsequent Chinese dynastic histories.

Qin's most feared general, responsible for the mass execution of roughly 400,000 Zhao prisoners after the Battle of Changping in 260 BCE. He won over 70 battles without a major defeat. His own king later forced him to suicide after Bai Qi refused to lead a campaign he considered unwinnable.

Zhao's most effective general during the early phase of Changping (260 BCE), who held Qin to a costly standoff for three years through defensive strategy. Qin agents spread disinformation to have him replaced by the inexperienced Zhao Kuo — directly causing the Zhao catastrophe that followed.

Qin's senior general during the wars of unification, who demanded 600,000 troops for the Chu campaign when the king offered 200,000. He proved correct: his patient year-long encirclement wore down Chu's army before a decisive battle. Wang Jian led Qin's most difficult conquests, including Zhao and Chu.

The heir of the Yan kingdom who sponsored Jing Ke's assassination attempt on Ying Zheng in 227 BCE. Dan had himself been held as a hostage at the Qin court and bore a personal grudge. After the attempt failed, his own father King Xi killed him as a peace offering to Qin — which Qin accepted and then conquered Yan anyway.
